en: The Splendor of the Victorious King’s Majesty.
This glorious region of Siṃhala stands upon the excavation made by the sons of Sagara;
it shines like a lover dancing with passion.
Touching the young maiden with the upper parts of his own hands.
This earth, thrice-traversed by the Buddhas in succession,
belongs to Vibhīṣaṇa, the sovereign lord of the Yakṣas and ruler of Laṅkā, for he has never broken his bond of affection.
Right here, the daughter of Janaka was made.
Śākyamuni himself composed these great instructions known as the Laṅkāvatāra right here,
in which his supreme compassion for others shines forth.
It is joined with the prohibition of eating the flesh of sentient beings. || 3 ||
Having conquered the yakṣas,
he who was self-conquered achieved victory here in the Dharma;
having established himself in the Dharma right here, he brought them into union.
Mahendra, together with his sister, was accompanied by jewels. ||4||
Having lived here on earth as a friend of Kumāradāsa, the wise Kālidāsa attained another body despite being without fault.
Having completed this beautiful poetic challenge, alas! || 5 ||
Seeing his friend deceased here, Kumāradāsa had no other remedy than to burn his own body in the funeral pyre.
Having cast [it] away, he became free from debt to his friend regarding that debt. || 6 ||
The Dharma of the Jina, which was taught here in Magadha as the root,
has been correctly set forth here in its explanations from the very beginning.
He shines forth in the recitations of the Buddha’s voice. || 7 ||
This ground stands as a treasure-repository, enriched with various jewels of great value,
and it is also filled with human gems.
By various kinds of those possessing supernatural powers. || 8 ||
Delightful with many villages and cities,
and graced by various kinds of gardens and groves,
it laughs at heaven, which is possessed of only a single city.
And seeing her distressed by that single forest... || 9 ||
The villages were delightful with trees laden with fruit and pleasing with lovely, tender creepers;
they were dear to the eyes with their verdant regions.
The cities exist one above the other. || 10 ||
Indeed, the dwellings of houses in the village were naturally constructed as pleasant abodes,
such that the citizens, merely by seeing them, [felt at ease].
They disparage happiness that must be achieved through great effort. || 11 ||
"Indeed, people here today say that among all villages, the one called Nedungamūva is the most delightful;
there is truly no other place as excellent as it."
Regarding this, they say that its etymological explanation is indeed [as follows].
Furthermore, it was filled with betel nuts, mangoes, and coconut fruits,
as well as with the charming and abundant fruits of the kandalī trees.
He describes his own prosperity here by means of jackfruit trees. || 13 ||
I think they say with joy that this very abundance of food will continue here as it turns back;
for even without words, the [fruits] are turning dark.
He whose fields produce rice.
For garments that are beautiful to behold, which possess a lovely luster due to their fresh youthfulness, constantly captivate the minds of young men wherever they are worn.
The dark-complexioned women moved along the path under some pretext. || 15 ||
Having purified their garments and bodies through vows,
those who have entered the abode of the Jinas at nightfall do not abandon it, even though their hearts are moist with devotion.
Young men [gaze upon] the casting of side-long glances by a young woman. || 16 ||
Even when observing the most exquisite states of passion in certain youths despite their advanced age,
people become joyful indeed out of affection for such beauty.
Surely the leaves [of the tree] are [being nourished] by the sap of that which is dry. || 17 ||
When one is established in awakening, someone places many wicks together in a single lamp-vessel;
I believe this is because of the excellent light arising from them.
to behold his own beloved as she moved along. || 18 ||
A certain woman, out of fear, follows the Sugata who has been born here after abandoning his beloved wife as he sets out toward Kāntā to pay him homage.
Desiring to bring about the return of her beloved. || 19 ||
As long as this body is maintained here, there is no completion of our task;
come, come, let us go to the abodes of the Sugatas.
By which the mind becomes pure there for a moment. || 20 ||
Having seen the sacred form of the Jina’s image,
there is no one here in this world who does not stand [in awe],
even as far as the abodes of the Sugatas.
By the grasping of moral discipline, past evil departs and new merit always arises; thus,
through a mind of supreme devotion here in this world.
In an instant, people proclaim one's virtue. || 22 ||
In this world, a moment of Dharma is extremely brief,
while a moment of dispute is of great duration;
all one's life passes away in [the pursuit of] Dharma and wealth.
And among people, [there arise] diseases and physical humors. || 23 ||
Having thus awakened his friend with these words,
while he contemplated nothing other than reality in his heart,
someone eager drew him toward the temple of the Jina.
Under a pretext, in order to show her own beloved woman. || 24 ||
(These five form a *kulaka*): Those youths who, even through instruction in the Dharma, do not attain a state of graceful refinement;
How could they not make the days filled with passion upon attaining the spring season? || 25 ||
Wherein he dwells forever in a concealed form, shining with abundant splendor,
yet only occasionally manifests his presence.
He [was delighted] by the *kuhū-ru* sound among the rows of mango trees.
Where the god Indra repeatedly discharges rainbows while raining, he spreads only the delusions of the monsoon,
so that water may be easily obtained.
Bringing down divine nectar here upon the earth. || 27 ||
The grace of the other seasons, overwhelmed at every moment by the rising of spring and the rains,
is like the union of a crow with a rhythmic beat.
Wherein only the same [nature] is observed. || 28 ||
Having conquered the cold, autumn becomes manifest here with the brilliance of ripened rice,
its nature transformed by the presence of spring.
Even without the juices of mangoes of delightful flavor. || 29 ||
Then, at that very time, in this place where the great Dharma prevails, he heard the sound of the *sāraṇa* reed-flutes.
At such a moment as this, he was overcome with intense longing.
He descended into the lineage of Vikramārka. || 30 ||
In this year [marked by] the Nidhi, Vasu, and Indu (1889),
in the month of Nidhi, that one who is as beautiful as the moon appeared.
Christ spread joy for your mother. || 31 ||
A suckling infant, holding onto his mother’s hand,
having reached the syllable *ḷ* or *ṛ* at her ear— this,
I believe, is for that purpose within the collection of the Vedic syllables.
The rule has separately taught the vowel *ḷ*.

Having heard the speech consisting of the great vital breaths (*mahāprāṇa*), Sarasvatī extended her voice through those [consonants] such as *gha, jha, ḍha, dha, bha, tha*, which consist of the minor vital breaths (*alpapāṇa*).
In this world, the Siṃhalas possess very little life-force. || 33 ||
In his childhood, while writing the letters of the alphabet and reading the pure numbers of Mount Meru,
he constantly brought satisfaction to his teacher.
Bestowing joy upon both his father and his mother. ||34||
Speaking, he shone with sounds enriched by his own language, by those of the local people, and by those arising from all of them;
for here, the well-spoken words reside within his heart.
With his charming body emitting [light], he shone forth. || 35 ||
In the village, indeed, with measured speech toward his elders, his self refined and young in age,
he desired to attain excellence.
He arrived at the abode where knowledge arises. || 36 ||
Having come together through the acquisition of knowledge, they made him— who was a resident of Hikkaḍḍuva, of noble form, highly auspicious, and bringing about blessings— their preceptor.
And one who possesses his own human [attendants] and one who possesses celestial chariots (vimāna). || 37 ||
The supreme physician who [heals] the ailments of the mind, the follower of the Dharma, the ornament of the Śākya clan—
his words here are of great significance.
She held it in her heart with great effort. || 38 ||
He developed an intense longing for that science of medicine, the sole treatise for the welfare of the world, which was proclaimed by the preeminent sages headed by Ātreya.
In that which accomplishes the true goal and is exceedingly easy to achieve. || 39 ||
He adopted speech originating from his own country for the sake of the people, which was graced by the quality of elegance,
as if it were his own learning acquired solely for the purpose of expounding it.
Shining with the power of the physician. || 40 ||
Having acquired knowledge during the best of his youth,
over a vast number of autumns,
he proceeded to the delightful [hermitage], shining with splendor.
Indeed, through the increase of wisdom, one truly attains the designation of "learned. || 41 ||
Having attained his station, he did not succumb to pride;
observing the commencement of his task, he did not look for mastery of the scriptures; seeing himself rising up like a bird, he gazed upon his own self.
Desiring to swallow the sky that has a blue appearance. ||42||
Countless people have set out upon this unprecedented path of Sarasvatī;
yet, not a single person has attained it.
Nor shall he attain its full enumeration in its entirety.
The mathematics seen by children begins with one and so forth,
yet it can be conceived even up to the limit of a *parārdha*;
however, the wise say that for this [mathematics], there is no beginning.
The wise do not speak of an end in reality. || 44 ||
Those who here enumerate the principles beginning with the elements (bhūtādi), citing them as substantial entities,
perceive only the atom and ultimately [discover] its disintegration.
They become filled with wonder, their faces turned toward emptiness. || 45 ||
Those who are highly proficient declare that consciousness is the beginning and the reality, for with a firm mind they perceive that all this external world is indeed devoid of consciousness.
Having beheld them, they enter into a state of deep sleep as it were.
Even while explaining the reality of sound and the other [objects] here,
one who perceives this entire world as consisting of external objects becomes deluded in this life due to the failure to attain the stainless [reality].
From recitation, one who asserts the self to consist of sound becomes even more powerful. || 47 ||
Having seen even Dhanvantari speaking of the reality of the humors and so forth of the body,
yet not actually demonstrating it through direct perception,
[the king] remained silent.
Who here could possibly undertake a discussion on the end of knowledge? || 48 ||
Having not visualized the mastery of the treatises within one's heart, but having observed only a single portion of them, one attempts to carry out the entire practice with one's own intellect.
He became inclined toward the worldly path. || 49 ||
Having observed the greatness of the scribes and having exerted effort here in the examination of the scribes' work,
the wise one emerged victorious.
For he is truly peerless among those who bring about liberation. || 51 ||
Desiring to know truly the livelihood and the science of physicians,
I have come here, for physicians are not found elsewhere in the world.
Bhiṣaja-pravāla went to the land of Vaṅga. || 52 ||
Taking up the water of the mouths of the Gaṅgā as they swiftly join him with their own faces,
the Lord of the Oceans shines resplendent as he sports.
In whatever region there is constant turbulence; || 53 ||
At this confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Lord of Waters, even those who have performed their ablutions there, though they be unwise, Indra—
accompanied by all the gods— welcomes at the gateway to heaven.
Having arrived through merit, he stands desiring to speak. || 54 ||
Adorned with clusters of lotuses and crossroads that possess a dark-green hue,
[the city] resounds with the sweet warbling of birds.
Where the lakes resound with the cries of waterfowl. || 55 ||
And where the lotus-born ponds, with their abundant waters and living fish,
proclaim the prosperity of those born of noble lineage.
Establishing his own presence in every house.
In that enchanting region,
there was a vast city with many-shaped halls,
uniquely beautiful as the dwelling place of Śambhu’s beloved.
He dwelt happily with Kālikā. || 57 ||
Within five years here,
he brought five branches of knowledge to perfection, and having mastered all the sciences, he accomplished his tasks.
Through his efforts, the wise-minded one became accomplished. || 58 ||
The eminent physician named Śrī Yāminībhūṣaṇa Rāya, a steadfast man among those who speak,
became the teacher of this [author], who was quick to grasp [his lessons].
Shining with the excellence of knowledge. || 59 ||
He became highly proficient in the *Suśruta*, having attained sharpness of intellect; being discerning, he applied the entire scripture to the practical performance of medical procedures.
Then, with great effort, he assumed the identity of Vāgbhaṭa.
Thus, at the age of thirty-two, he who was designated by the title "Jewel among Physicians" shone forth,
his person adorned by the majesty of that jewel.
He became capable of extracting [the world] from its defects. || 61 ||
Then, being both capable and devoted, he bowed down at each and every place where the Blessed One,
whose mind was filled with compassion, had dwelt while teaching throughout the worlds.
Surrounded by his own disciples, he [performed] his own duty well.
Holy is Gayā in Magadha,
which is declared among people to be purified by the dust of the feet of that venerable Great Bodhi tree.
Praising her, he became happy. || 63 ||
On that tree beneath which the ornament of the Śākya clan removed the state of being blinded by intoxication belonging to Māra,
he attained the name "Buddha" and became the Teacher.
With his inner self deeply bowed, he prostrated before him.
For one who has no other refuge here in the world of men, there shall be auspicious progress and happiness;
[that refuge is] the city named Vārāṇasī, which is sacred.
Then, having approached, she was seen by those wise ones who had come there as her protectors.
Being unable to traverse the entire vast territory of Bharata,
he created this very land with great effort so that it might be seen.
Dhātṛ [created] the city, which was a reflection of that [city]. || 66 ||
Near Pūri, because it is protected by the essence of the Dharma through the instruction of the Sugata,
Rudra does not leave his dwelling.
It is said that Sāranātha [was established] out of devotion to the Buddha. || 67 ||
Having indeed gone to this sacred ground called Ṛṣipattana, situated between the rivers Mṛgadhārā and Aruṇā,
with his own head bowed low in prostration—
Exalted, he shone forth exceedingly. || 68 ||
Having reached the final playground of the Sugata in Kuśinagarī, he of the purified mind rolled upon the earth,
his limbs prostrate.
With his soul overflowing with tears, he rained them forth out of devotion.
Thus, having purified the ground of his mind, he returned once more to his own stage; having acquired knowledge from his teachers like a wise man, he was established in his own domain.
He has undertaken creation for the sake of spreading knowledge.
Indeed, the primary seat of medicine was established at Gamphāpura by one who was self-originated and proficient;
disciples arrived there from the four directions.
They stood surrounding him on all sides. || 71 ||
Today, he is possessed of great renown and endowed with all riches, accompanied by disciples here who are disciplined by their learning;
he is the foremost among the editors of Caraka.
He became a member of the assembly in the king's court. || 72 ||
The authorized successor appointed by Śrī Dāsagupta,
who followed the path of Gandhi in his own life,
attained the status of a Guru upon the rise of knowledge.
The sovereign of physicians shines forth. || 73 ||
May he enjoy manifold pleasures in this world,
whether celestial or terrestrial;
may he always yoke his own mind to virtuous deeds.
Living upon the earth for hundreds of autumns. || 74 ||
In the land of Siṃhaladvīpa, renowned for its peerless and constant exposition of wisdom, and here in another hermitage of the Sugatas known by the name Vidyālaṅkāra— there,
a twice-born man was initiated into the excellent doctrine of the Śramaṇas by the venerable Śrī Dharmānanda.
May this foot of Vikramāditya indeed bring joy to Śāntibhikṣu among men. 75.

Thus ends *Vikramārccipadyam*, the work of Paṇḍita Śrī Śāntibhikṣu Śāstrin, Sāhityācārya and Mahācārya of Saṃskṛta at Vidyālaṅkāra University; a disciple of the venerable Śrī Dharmānanda Nāyakapāda who lived abroad in Siṃhala with his wife and son; and a resident of the village of Bībīpur near Lakṣmaṇapura in Kosala, Northern India, who received the degree of Doctor from the University of Leipzig.
Auspicious!
The elapsed years since the Buddha's passing are 2510.
Of those phenomena that arise from causes, the Tathāgata has explained their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa.
